title: Tokens ↔ Neurons ↔ Memory Processes
content_html:
Tokens ↔ Neurons ↔ Memory Processes

This explainer maps the discrete-symbol world of large language models (LLMs) to the distributed-dynamics of biological memory. It offers three layered diagrams—encoding, storage, and retrieval—plus a succinct comparison and references.

Token: Smallest processed unit in an LLM (subword/word/character), mapped to a vector via an embedding table.

Embedding: Dense vector representation capturing usage-driven semantics; analogous to neural population codes.

Attention: Mechanism computing inter-token influence; parallels selective attention and working-memory gating.

Hippocampal Indexing: Rapidly formed links that enable pattern completion and episodic recall; cortex consolidates semantics.

Tokens in LLMs are not like individual neurons. They are closer to symbolic fragments (e.g., subwords), while embeddings + attention parallel distributed neural population codes and dynamic routing.

Summary

LLM Brain Implication for “Memory”
Tokens (discrete) Features across neurons (continuous) Tokens ≈ symbolic fragments, not neurons
Embeddings Population codes Most direct representational parallel
Attention over context Working-memory gating; oscillatory control Dynamic routing of information
Trained weights (static post‑training) Synaptic plasticity (lifelong) LLM “semantic memory” is baked-in; human memory remains plastic
No true episodic traces Episodic traces via hippocampal indexing LLMs lack personal episodic recall
